short: A 16-bit float format (1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa bits) whose raw bits can be read as integer words.
long: bfloat16 keeps float32's 8-bit exponent but only 7 mantissa bits, so it stores model weights in half the space. Reading each weight as a raw uint16 lets you compare files bit for bit and pick out fields such as the exponent. Flipping the lowest mantissa bit changes a weight by well under 1%.

short: Comparing a fine-tuned model to its exact base model, tensor by tensor, to isolate what the author changed.
long: A fine-tuned model is its base plus changes. With the exact base model in hand, every word that differs is the author's work, and every identical tensor was left alone. Comparing raw bit patterns instead of values means rounding can't hide a change.

short: The lookup table with one row of numbers per token id. Rarely used rows make handy hidden storage.
long: When a language model reads a token it fetches that token's row from the embedding matrix. Rows for rare tokens, or for ids past the end of the real vocabulary, are barely trained or never used. An author can overwrite them with data without changing the model's behaviour much.

short: Hiding message bits in the least significant bits of numbers or pixels, where changes are too small to notice.
long: The lowest bit of a number carries the least information, so overwriting it with a message bit barely changes anything visible. ZyGPT's variant defines each payload bit as the carrier's LSB XOR the base model's LSB at a secret position, so the untouched base model is needed to read it.

short: A SHA-3 extendable-output function used to turn a secret seed into a reproducible list of hiding positions.
long: SHAKE-256 takes any input and produces as many pseudo-random bytes as requested. Cut into integers and reduced modulo the number of eligible slots, those bytes become positions. Anyone with the seed regenerates the same positions. Without it, you can't tell where the payload bits are.

short: Authenticated encryption rejects wrong keys or wrong ciphertext, so each brute-force guess verifies itself.
long: AES-GCM appends a 16-byte authentication tag that only the correct key and untouched ciphertext reproduce. A wrong guess fails the check, with a false-pass chance around 2^-128. That makes brute force a clean yes/no experiment with no risk of accepting a fake answer.

short: Multiply the search space by the cost per guess before deciding whether a brute force is feasible.
long: Counting the space first tells you whether a search is feasible or hopeless. Choosing 5 of 69 records is 11.2 million keys, about an hour and a half at 1,900 keys per second. Every subset of 69 is 2^69, which nothing finishes. Usually it's the details of the mechanism that shrink a hopeless space into a feasible one.

short: Running your method on a case where the answer is known to be present, to prove it can find it.
long: If a search or test cannot recover a target you planted yourself, its failure to find the real target means nothing. A passing positive control is what makes a null result interpretable. Psychology calls a close cousin of this a manipulation check.

short: Writing the opening of a chat model's reply yourself so it never reaches the point where it would refuse.
long: Refusal is mostly decided at the first token of the assistant's turn. If you render the chat template, append your own opening and remove the end-of-turn marker, you hand the model a sentence already in progress. It breaks refusals reliably. It can't make a model produce knowledge it doesn't have.

short: Making a chat model write the user's next turn, where no refusal training applies.
long: Secrecy training is attached to the assistant role. If you let the model generate the user's side of a conversation, seeded as someone who already knows the secret, the guard may not apply. It is one of the strongest black-box methods in Cywiński et al. (2025).

short: A prefill attack in a language the fine-tune probably did not cover, to reach base-model behaviour.
long: Safety and persona tuning is often done mainly in one language and carries over imperfectly to others. Prefilling in another language can fall back to base-model behaviour. Base models confabulate in every language, though, so you need the same prefill after an unrelated question as a control.

short: A gradient-guided search for an adversarial token string that makes a model produce a chosen output.
long: GCG (Zou et al., 2023) uses gradients to shortlist token substitutions and keeps those that raise the probability of a target output. It can find triggers a human would never type. It only raises confidence in an output you specify, so it can't produce a string the model never learned.

short: Training raw input embedding vectors by gradient descent to steer a model's output.
long: Instead of searching over real tokens, you optimise a few continuous vectors fed in place of token embeddings. This is a strictly larger search space than any typeable prompt. If even an optimised soft prompt yields only placeholders, the target is very unlikely to be reachable from the input side.

short: Projecting a model's intermediate activations through its output vocabulary to see what each layer is leaning towards.
long: The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) decodes the residual stream at every layer as if it were the final one. A secret that later layers suppress can show up mid-stack. For exact-string secrets it is one of the most effective elicitation methods in the literature.

short: Adding a computed direction to a model's activations to push its behaviour one way.
long: Take the average activation difference between two behaviours and add it during generation to shift the model towards one of them. It can bring back behaviours a fine-tune suppressed. The direction has to be cleaned of confounds such as language, or it steers the wrong thing.

short: Scoring tokens by how much more a fine-tuned model prefers them than its base model does.
long: Running the fine-tuned and base models together and amplifying their difference picks out what the fine-tune learned. A memorised string should stay stable as the amplification grows, while confabulation drifts. It's a white-box way to read what an adapter added.

short: Fine-tuning by adding a small low-rank update to each weight matrix instead of retraining it.
long: Low-rank adaptation adds a rank-r matrix to each targeted weight. After merging, the difference from the base has exactly r significant singular values, which makes it detectable and fully enumerable. Reading those directions shows everything the fine-tune changed.

short: Applying a fine-tune in reverse (base minus the update) to delete its trained behaviour.
long: Rebuilding each weight as base + alpha times the fine-tune delta, with alpha = -1, removes the trained behaviour instead of bypassing it. If a guard were hiding knowledge, deleting the guard this way should expose it. On ZyGPT it exposed a base model that did not know what a CTF flag was.

short: Separating whether a model stops refusing from whether it can then produce the real target.
long: Jailbreak reports often treat a broken refusal as a successful extraction. They're different quantities. Willingness is how often the model answers, and capability is how often the answer is verifiably right. High willingness with zero capability is a real result in its own right.

short: With zero events in n trials, the 95% upper bound on the true rate is about 3/n.
long: A quick way to put a number on 'it never happened' (Hanley & Lippman-Hand, 1983). Zero successes in 350 independent extraction attempts bounds the true success rate at 0.86%. It assumes the trials are independent and representative, so diverse strategies matter.

short: Whether asking the same question again gives the same answer; used to probe whether a model holds a string.
long: A psychometric idea: a reliable measure is consistent across repetitions. If a model really holds a secret, repeated questions about its properties should agree. The design only works if a control condition with a known answer is answered correctly first.
